qset.question: Using the calendar-year Nifty 50 TR returns in Exhibit 10, suppose an investment was worth Rs. 100 at the start of 2008 and remained invested through the end of 2009, with no deposits or withdrawals. Did the 2009 rebound fully recover the 2008 loss? Calculate the approximate ending value and cumulative percentage return using compounded annual returns.
qset.answer: No. The return was -51.27% in 2008 and +77.59% in 2009. The ending value is Rs. 100 × (1 - 0.5127) × (1 + 0.7759) = approximately Rs. 86.54. The cumulative return is approximately -13.46%, so the rebound did not fully recover the loss.

qset.question: Using the March 2020 and March 2024 endpoints in Exhibit 17, which grew faster in percentage terms: Nifty 50 ETF AUM or Nifty 50 index-fund AUM? Calculate the approximate percentage growth of each, rather than comparing their plotted heights or absolute increases.
qset.answer: Index-fund AUM grew faster in percentage terms. ETF AUM increased from Rs. 726 billion to Rs. 2,775 billion, giving (2775 - 726) / 726 × 100 ≈ 282.23% growth. Index-fund AUM increased from Rs. 53 billion to Rs. 522 billion, giving (522 - 53) / 53 × 100 ≈ 884.91% growth.

qset.question: The index-performance text says that the Nifty 50 Total Return index assumes dividends are reinvested and reports a 14.10% annualized return since June 30, 1999. An analyst treats that 14.10% as price appreciation alone and adds a separate dividend return to estimate total return. Is this valid, and can the price-only annualized return be determined from the 14.10% figure alone? Explain.
qset.answer: No. The 14.10% is already a total-return figure incorporating price return and reinvested dividends, so adding a separate dividend return would double-count the dividend component. The price-only annualized return cannot be determined from that total-return figure alone without additional information about the dividend component or the price-return series.
